sections.html:
No city in North Dakota has more people than Fargo, which is also the Cass County seat. It stands on the Red River's west bank, with Moorhead, Minnesota, opposite, and the combined Fargo-Moorhead metro is the state's biggest urban area. Permits and taxes depend on whether your parcel falls in Fargo, West Fargo or unincorporated Cass County, so settle that first.

The city dates to 1871. In 1893 a fire destroyed 31 downtown blocks, which were rebuilt within a year, and a tornado in 1957 flattened much of the north end. Houses in the older neighborhoods therefore differ widely from newer ones in age and construction, and buyers price that gap.

sections.h2: The Red River and your sale
sections.html:
A big part of Fargo real estate carries flood risk, which shapes insurance, lending and buyer interest. The National Weather Service measured a 1997 crest of 39.72 feet at Fargo, 2.42 feet over the 1969 record of 37.3 feet. The 2009 crest hit 40.84 feet, and the city had bought 700 houses in flood-prone areas by 2012.

The FM Area Diversion Project is meant to protect nearly 260,000 people, with permanent protection expected by 2027. Its website covers land acquisition and flood insurance status. A house near the river should be checked against the mapped floodplain, and against the diversion project's footprint, before you list.

Winters matter too. January averages 9.2 degrees Fahrenheit, about 43 days a year reach 0 or lower, and snowfall averages 51.4 inches. Roof snow load, basement moisture and heating are sensible checks before listing. If water has entered the basement, say so and share the repair records.

Fargo's Inspections Department enforces the International Property Maintenance Code and Land Development Code Chapter 20 on rentals. It asks owners to record their rentals with the department at no charge. If you own a rental you plan to sell, expect a letter to the mailing address on Cass County tax records.

Inspectors look at a specific list, and a buyer's inspector will flag the same items:

  • Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and deadbolts on entry doors
  • Stair guards, graspable handrails and peeling exterior paint
  • Bathroom and dryer ventilation, window condition and bedroom egress
  • Overcrowding, with a limit of three unrelated tenants

Owners have five business days to change a scheduled inspection date, and unanswered requests can lead to an exterior inspection and fees. The department deals with health and safety, not lease or eviction disputes.

sections.h2: Special assessments and what they mean for a sale
sections.html:
Fargo pays contractors as work is built, then pools the cost of projects about once a year and sells a Special Assessment Revenue Bond. Property owners repay it through yearly special assessment payments. Water main replacement and flood protection are examples of work funded this way. An annual installment appears on your tax statement.

To see what a parcel owes, look it up on FargoParcels.com, request a payoff amount through the city's online form, or call the Special Assessment Division at 701.241.1326. Ask the division and your title company who carries the balance at sale, and get the answer in writing before you set a closing date.

Cass County bills real estate tax on the state schedule. Pay in full by February 15 for a 5 percent discount on the consolidated tax, or pay half plus special assessments by March 1 and the rest by October 15. Specials and drain taxes are not discounted.

Charge or eventCass County rule
First installment penalty3% on March 1, May 1, July 1 and October 15
Second installment penalty6% if unpaid after October 15
Prior-year delinquent tax1% interest per month
Tax saleThird Tuesday in November, 10:00 a.m.

All current-year property taxes must be paid in full before a deed transferring ownership can be recorded. Bills go to the owner of record as of November 1. The Finance Office is at the Cass County Courthouse, 211 9th Street South, Fargo, phone (701) 241-5600. When the house sells, the closing statement or title company settles who pays what.

sections.h2: What to line up before closing
sections.html:
Three records can hold up a Fargo closing: the mortgage payoff, the special assessment balance and the Cass County tax status. Each comes from a different office, so request them early.

  • A payoff letter from your lender
  • The special assessment payoff amount from the city's Special Assessment Division
  • Confirmation from the Cass County Finance Office that current-year taxes are paid, since the deed cannot be recorded until they are
  • Floodplain status for the parcel, and any rental inspection letters if the house has tenants

With these in hand, a cash or financed buyer can move quickly, and you can see what you will net before you commit to a date.

Fargo owners can list, sell privately or accept a cash offer, and the right choice depends on the house and the timeline. A listed sale usually involves repairs, showings and a buyer's loan approval, while a cash purchase takes the house as it stands.

Whichever you pick, North Dakota's disclosure law (Century Code 47-10-02.1) requires sellers of homes with up to four units to disclose material facts, usually before final acceptance of the purchase agreement. A cash offer can be a good idea when the house needs repairs, was inherited or is a tenant-occupied rental. Compare it with listing costs and timing before you decide.

A Fargo sale moves through the same few steps whichever route you take. Once you accept an offer, a title company opens a file and orders the payoff figures. The lender gives a payoff letter. The Special Assessment Division gives the city balance. The Cass County Finance Office confirms that current-year taxes are paid, because the deed cannot be recorded otherwise.

Floodplain status comes up next, particularly near the river, and a rental brings inspection letters into the file. If any of these records conflict with your own, sort it out now, before the closing date, so nothing is left to clear at the table. On closing day the title company pays the lender, the city and the county from your proceeds, you sign the deed and the sale is recorded.

A cash purchase skips the buyer's loan approval and lender appraisal, which are the two steps most likely to push a closing date back. It also skips repair negotiations, since the buyer takes the house as it stands. A house with a damp basement, an old furnace or a roof that needs work can still sell, and the cost of those problems is built into one offer.

The county and city steps do not change. Taxes, special assessments and the mortgage are still paid at closing. What changes is the number of people who must approve the deal and the time it takes. That matters if you are selling a tenant-occupied rental, settling an estate or trying to close ahead of a penalty date.

faqs.q: When did the Red River last set a record at Fargo?
faqs.a: The 2009 crest of 40.84 feet is the record, above the 1997 crest of 39.72 feet. Check the National Weather Service for current river data.

faqs.q: Do I need to pay off Fargo special assessments before selling?
faqs.a: Ask the Special Assessment Division at 701.241.1326 and your title company who carries the balance at sale. You can request a payoff amount through the city's form.

faqs.q: Who gets the Cass County tax bill in a sale?
faqs.a: Bills go to the owner of record as of November 1. Check the closing statement or ask your title company who pays which part of the year.

faqs.q: Does Fargo require a rental license?
faqs.a: Fargo asks owners to record rentals with the Inspections Department, which is free. Inspectors then check the property against the maintenance code.

faqs.q: Is a cash offer a good idea in Fargo?
faqs.a: It can be when the house needs repairs, is inherited or is a tenant-occupied rental. Compare it with listing costs and timing before you decide.
